summary: InterNauticos: Orbit Lab and its student portal, InterNauticos: Orbit Lab — Explorer, form an interactive educational ecosystem built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to bridge the gap between abstract space facts and real engineering trade-offs for students ages 7–12 and their teachers. We developed a browser-based learning portal paired with a mission control simulator and a structured Educator Study Guide. Through this platform, students progress across four accessible phases—Design, Build, Launch, and Explore—playing either solo or in four-player cooperative teams composed of a Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms Officer. Instead of offering risk-free choices, every engineering decision carries real consequences across six critical resources: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission lifetime. Grounded in NASA open datasets—including DONKI for space weather and radiation risks, and OSDR for astronaut health parameters—the simulator provides causal feedback explaining why a mission succeeds or fails. Requiring zero downloads or expensive hardware, this accessible platform empowers teachers to integrate hands-on STEM problem-solving into any classroom, turning young learners into active, data-literate critical thinkers.
details:
The development of educational projects in the aerospace field frequently faces the challenge of simplifying complex concepts without losing scientific rigor. To address this need within the framework of the NASA Space Apps Challenge, InterNauticos: Orbit Lab was designed alongside its student portal, InterNauticos: Orbit Lab — Explorer, an interactive ecosystem conceived for students ages 7–12 and their teachers. This project's main objective is to bridge the gap between abstract spatial data and real engineering decisions through a playful and educational experience. 

Regarding its operation, the platform guides users through a structured four-phase workflow: Design, where mission objectives are established; Build, focused on selecting spacecraft components and scientific payloads; Launch, dedicated to choosing orbits and compatible launch vehicles; and Explore, in which the mission is simulated and telemetry is analyzed. Participants can play individually or in cooperative teams of up to four members, taking on specialized roles such as Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms Officer, which encourages negotiation and the joint management of six critical resources: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission lifetime.

Among the system's most prominent benefits is its causal feedback approach, which explains in detail why a mission fails—such as battery depletion during an eclipse or insufficient bandwidth—instead of simply displaying a generic error screen. Additionally, as a fully web-based platform accessible without downloads or prior registrations, it eliminates technical barriers and integrates easily into any school environment through an Educator Study Guide.

The project's creativity is manifested in the rigorous use of NASA open data, integrating space weather metrics from the DONKI database and biological parameters from OSDR, which endows the simulation with scientific authenticity. Its dual-interface design separates the friendly children's exploration narrative from the technical control and simulation panels. During its conception, the team strictly considered factors such as children's cognitive load, the interdependence of design variables, and equity in technological access. Developed using web technologies and publicly hosted on Netlify, this project seeks to transform young students into data-literate critical thinkers prepared to lead the future of space exploration.
